# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-16 (Extended v125)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Winter Year 4—Louis Philippe's reign)**: Paris—Gorbeau house (50-52, Salpêtrière district); Luxembourg gardens; le Petit-Picpus convent; M. Gillenormand's residences; English provincial towns (Dunstead, Staveford, Kelmere, Torton, Ostcombe, Ravenmere, Kelford, Yarlby, Gulhaven, Wilwick, Wilholt, Quenford). **Environmental details**: Rain threatened since morning, held off. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Road all ruts and puddles after thaw. Light went early. Frost silvered hedges overnight. Icy breeze; wind off water carries salt/tar scent. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. Baker's boy late; line at oven grew long. Children chased hoop down lane.

## Primary Locations
**GORBEAU HOUSE**: 50-52 Salpêtrière district. **JONDRETTE DEN**: Abject, fetid, sordid. Furniture: straw chair, infirm table, crockery, two pallets, straw beds. Walls: leprous, seamed, obscene charcoal sketches, repulsive moisture. Fireplace with brazier filled burning charcoal (glowing hot, red with blue flame), pot, broken boards, suspended rags, bird-cage. Dormer window (four broken panes). Colored engraving "THE DREAM" (sleeping woman/child, eagle, Napoleon on blue column). **Wooden panel—Battle of Waterloo painting: sergeant rescuer (Thénardier) carrying colonel victim (Pontmercy) amid smoke.** Two heaps: old iron/ropes and rope-ladder with wooden rungs and two hooks. Verdigris candlestick with burning candle.

## Crisis at Gorbeau House: Sequence and Resolution
**M. Leblanc's initial struggle**: Overturned chair and table, moved toward window with prodigious agility. Six robust fists seized him—three "chimney-builders" dragged him back. Thénardier woman wound hands in his hair. Herculean struggle: M. Leblanc knocked old man tumbling, overthrew two more with backward hand sweeps. Four others seized him by both arms and back of neck.

**M. Leblanc bound with ropes**: Despite binding, surrounded, half plunged in grave, M. Leblanc remained impassive—soul inaccessible to terror. Preserved silence, carried precaution of forgetting anxiety for own life. **Marius found this superbly melancholy visage and extraordinary composure deeply troubling.**

**Thénardier's metamorphosis**: Transformed from ferocious robber into polished negotiator—moderated language, subdued, crafty, reserved, choice diction. **Thénardier's scheme**: Wife will dress as before and hunt up "the Lark" (Cosette) with letter from M. Leblanc. Girl will follow into carriage. Outside barrier, trap with two horses waits. Young lady will alight from fiacre; Thénardier's comrade will enter other vehicle with her; wife returns to report completion. **Threat**: "If you have me arrested, my comrade will give a turn of his thumb to the Lark, that's all." Thénardier avoided naming girl—precaution of clever man.

**M. Leblanc's extraordinary act (turning point)**: Before seven men could collect senses, M. Leblanc bent down into fireplace, stretched out hand to brazier, straightened himself up. **Brandished above his head the red-hot chisel, emitting threatening glow**—almost free and in formidable attitude. Thénardier, female Thénardier, and ruffians huddled in amazement at extremity of hovel, stared in stupefaction.

**Means of escape**: Prisoner had coin piece on person when searched; contrived to conceal it in hand; having right hand free, unscrewed it and used as saw to cut cords—explaining faint noise Marius had observed.

**Marius's response**: Reeled in utter horror. Very ruffians shuddered. Hardly muscle of old man's face contracted. While red-hot iron sank into smoking wound, **impassive and almost august, he fixed on Thénardier his beautiful glance, in which there was no hatred, and where suffering vanished in serene majesty.**

**Javert's ambush and M. Leblanc's final escape**: Javert (tall man, square face, thin firm mouth, thick gray ferocious whiskers) positioned outside Gorbeau house with men. At nightfall, posted young girls as lookouts; "caged" Azelma—Éponine disappeared, not at post. Grew impatient, decided to go upstairs without waiting for Marius's pistol-shot signal. **Took action before Marius fired.** Ruffians terrified, flung themselves on arms abandoned in corners—one with meat-axe, another with key, another with bludgeon, rest with shears, pincers, hammers. Thénardier had knife in fist. **Thénardier woman snatched enormous paving-stone from angle of window (daughters' ottoman), hurled at Javert's head. Javert ducked; stone passed over him, struck wall behind.** **M. Leblanc's escape during chaos**: Door was guarded, but window was not. As soon as released from bonds and while Javert drawing up report, took advantage of confusion, crowd, darkness, moment when general attention diverted from him, to dash out of window.

## Marius Pontmercy: Crisis of Conscience (Unresolved)
**Identity and age**: Baron Marius Pontmercy, twenty years old; three years estranged from grandfather. **Paternal legacy**: Colonel's written instruction regarding baron title and Waterloo sergeant Thénardier. Lost medallion of black shagreen. **Now recognized**: Thénardier depicted in Waterloo painting—sergeant who rescued father at Waterloo.

**Unprecedented perplexity (evening crisis)**: For last hour had two voices in conscience—one enjoining him to respect father's testament, other crying to rescue prisoner. Two voices continued uninterrupted struggle tormenting him to agony. Up to that moment cherished vague hope of reconciling two duties, but nothing within limits of possibility presented itself. **Had not time for deliberation—scene hastening to catastrophe. He was on verge of swooning. Knees gave way beneath him. Last possibility of doubt vanished. Certainly was Thénardier of the will.**

**Critical moral dilemma**: Everything depended on Marius. Unknown to themselves, he held all beings in his hand. If he fired pistol, M. Leblanc saved, Thénardier lost; if he did not fire, M. Leblanc sacrificed. Remorse awaited him either case. Father once saved by Thénardier at Waterloo—sergeant rescued colonel. Yet M. Leblanc now victim of Thénardier's ambush. Moral obligation to both: honor father's will AND prevent crime against innocent man and Cosette's father. **Crisis of conscience at absolute peak; outcome unclear.**

## Girl (Cosette) and M. Leblanc Identity
**Girl identity clarified**: Handkerchief bore letters U. F., which meant Urbain Fabre. M. Leblanc is Monsieur Fabre—the girl's biological father. Cosette became convent scholar; believes Valjean is her father; adores him. **Marius now recognizes**: The "girl" he worshipped for six months is Cosette, whom he encountered again miraculously in hovel as charitable visitor with M. Leblanc. She is also being held captive by Thénardier's scheme.

## Jean Valjean
Valjean integrated as convent assistant gardener; inhabits old garden hut with Fauchelevent. Spiritual transformation complete. Fauchelevent sole ally aware of full presence.

## English Provincial Towns: Population Movements and Mundane Activities
**Population movements**: Peten Haskick broke faith with Luwyn Brackick; promised work (pay old debt owed to Prydenridge family) never begun. **Peten Haskick found work in Quenford, moved there, did not return to Staveford. Lura Haskick followed him to Quenford within the month.** **Kadrek went along to live in Wilholt.** **Only daughter of Zalis Corrley left Torton and settled in Wilholt.** **Before spring was out, Kadan Corrley took Yewyn Corrford in marriage at Kelmere. Couple lived in Kelmere from then on.** Stenworth and Prydenridge families: Pelde Stenson, Davus Stenworth, Fewyn Stenworth, Havus Stenworth, Dalis, Yera Stenworth, Nerine Prydenridge, Luvie Prydenridge, Zavus Prydenridge, Vesmira Thornmere, Wenelle Lindmere (gave up idleness, took work as chandler), Isric Thornmere.

**Daily activities and mundane events**: Sorting old letters, mending torn sleeves, scrubbing steps, humming childhood tunes. **Fewyn Stenworth argued with carter over price of sack of oats.** **Rorald argued with carter over price of sack of oats.** **Pelia Lindmere read the almanac aloud, mispronouncing half the saints.** **Pelia hummed a tune from childhood while scrubbing the step.** **Rovus Prydenridge hummed a tune from childhood while scrubbing the step.** Conversations: weather, harvest, lame horse, rain, river up, price of salt. Children chased hoop down lane, shrieking.

## Historical Context: The Restoration and Revolution of July (1815-1832)
**Bourbon Restoration critique**: After Napoleon fell, House of Bourbon returned to France. Believed it bestowed rights and could take back charter rights. Did not suspect roots of French society not fixed in Bourbons but in nations. Bourbons were illustrious and bleeding knot in history, but no longer principal element of destiny, necessary base of politics.

**Restoration's fatal decision (1830)**: Abruptly decided on plan of action and risked its stroke. One morning elevated voice, contested collective title and individual right of nation to sovereignty, of citizen to liberty. Denied to nation that which made it a nation, denied to citizen that which made him citizen.

**Fifteen years of intellectual progress (1815-1830)**: Under Restoration, nation had grown accustomed to calm discussion lacking under Republic, to grandeur in peace lacking under Empire. For fifteen years, great principles—equality before law, liberty of conscience, speech, press, accessibility of all aptitudes to all functions—could be seen at work in perfect peace. Thus it proceeded until 1830. **The Bourbons were instrument of civilization which broke in hands of Providence.**

**Revolution of July (1830)**: Had hardly produced shock; had not even paid vanquished royalty honor of treating it as enemy, shedding blood. In eyes of despotic governments, Revolution of July committed fault of being formidable and remaining gentle. Nothing attempted or plotted against it. Mysterious respect springs from events in which we sense collaboration of someone working above man.

**Philosophical reflection on Right vs. Fact**: Property of right is to remain eternally beautiful and pure. Fact, if exist only as fact, if contain only too little of right or none, infallibly destined to become deformed, impure, perhaps monstrous.

**Post-revolution necessity of dynasty**: After revolution, when part of monarchical continent, politicians claim first requirement is to procure dynasty. Dynasty conceals scaffolding, covers ambulance. King resulting from revolution may be and useful to be revolutionary—participant in own person in that revolution, lent hand to it, compromised or distinguished himself therein.

**Bourgeois aspiration after 1830**: State to which part of nation called bourgeoisie aspired after shock of 1830 was not inertia or slumber—was the halt.

## Louis Philippe (Winter Year 4)
**Character and reign**: Had been handsome, in old age remained graceful; not always approved by nation, always so by masses; he pleased. Lacked majesty; wore no crown although king, no white hair although old man. Manners belonged to old regime; habits to new—mixture of noble and bourgeois suited 1830. Transition reigning. Preserved ancient pronunciation and orthography placed at service of modern opinions. Loved Poland and Hungary but wrote _les Polonois_, pronounced _les Hongrais_. Wore uniform of national guard like Charles X., ribbon of Legion of Honor like Napoleon.

**Daily habits**: Went little to chapel, not at all to chase, never to opera. Incorruptible by sacristans, whippers-in, ballet-dancers—part of bourgeois popularity. Had no heart. Went out with umbrella under arm, which long formed part of aureole. Bit of mason, gardener, something of doctor; bled postilion who had tumbled from horse. No more went about without lancet than did Henri IV. without poniard. Royalists jeered—first king to shed blood with object of healing.

**Grievances deduced**: Democratic right confiscated, progress secondary interest, street protests violently repressed, military execution of insurrections. Rue Transnonain, counsels of war, absorption of real country by legal country on half shares with three hundred thousand privileged. Belgium refused, Algeria harshly conquered with more barbarism than civilization. Breach of faith to Abd-el-Kader, Blaye, Deutz bought, Pritchard paid. **Policy more domestic than national was doing of King.** Louis Philippe rather too much of paternal king; incubation of family with object of founding dynasty afraid of everything, does not like to be disturbed; hence excessive timidity displeasing to people. Had 14th of July in civil and Austerlitz in military tradition.

**Family virtues**: Deep tenderness toward family deserved by family. Domestic group worthy of admiration. Virtues dwelt side by side with talents. One daughter, Marie d'Orleans, placed name of race among artists as Charles d'Orleans placed it among poets. Made of soul marble named Jeanne d'Arc. Two daughters elicited from Metternich: "They are young people such as are rarely seen, and princes such as are never seen."

**Trace of Revolution**: Memory of Revolution like living imprint of great years, minute by minute. One day, in presence of witness, rectified from memory whole of letter A in alphabetical list of Constituent Assembly.

**Press and conscience**: King of broad daylight. While he reigned press was free, tribune was free, conscience and speech were free. Laws of September open to sight. Although fully aware of gnawing power of light on privileges, left throne exposed to light. History will do justice for this loyalty.

**Final judgment deferred**: Hour when history speaks with free and venerable accent has not yet sounded for him; moment has not come to pronounce definite judgment. Louis Blanc himself recently softened first verdict. Louis Philippe elected by two _almosts_: 221 and 1830 (half-Parliament and half-revolution). From superior point of view where philosophy must place itself, cannot judge except with certain reservations in name of absolute democratic principle. In eyes of absolute, outside right of man and right of people, all is usurpation. **Yet what can be said at present: that Louis Philippe, taken in himself, and from point of view of human goodness, will remain one of best princes who ever sat on throne.** A dead man testifying in king's favor; epitaph penned by dead man is sincere; one shade may console another shade.

**Divine text and interpretation**: God delivers visible will in events—obscure text written in mysterious tongue. Men make hasty, incorrect translations full of errors, gaps, nonsense. Very few minds comprehend divine language. Most sagacious, calmest, most profound decipher slowly; when arrive with text, task long completed; already twenty translations on public place. From each springs party; from each misinterpretation faction. Each party thinks it alone has true text; each faction possesses light.

**Revolutions vs. revolts**: Old parties who cling to heredity by grace of God think one has right to revolt against revolutions. Error. In these revolutions, one who revolts is not people; it is king. Revolution precisely contrary of revolt. Every revolution, being normal outcome, contains within itself its legitimacy, which false revolutionists sometimes dishonor, but which remains even when soiled, survives even when stained with blood.
